title: Why does automated flagging help? Sensitivity versus suspicion shift
hypothesis: Accurate detector labels raise accuracy relative to control and random labels; random labels increase AI-judgments without increasing accuracy.
comparison: Accurate labels vs random labels vs control; secondary: share of posts judged AI (bias), accuracy on real and AI posts separately
rationale: Automated Flagging raised total accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]) while the pooled effect was only +1.0 point and generic Flagging showed -1.0. This leaves open whether detector labels add information (better discrimination) or simply make people more suspicious of everything; the source reported fake and real accuracy separately but did not test the mechanism.
contribution: Separates informative-label (sensitivity) from label-presence (response bias) accounts of the automated flagging gain.
unresolved: Image files and label overlays must be supplied by the research team
IRB number and compensation to be set by the research team

title: Does the AI Literacy Guide effect hold for older adults and for audio-visual vs. still-image posts?
hypothesis: Both the Guide and automated flagging raise accuracy relative to control among adults 55+, with the Guide effect smaller than in the source study.
primary_outcome: Share of 12 posts correctly classified as AI-generated or real.
comparison: Each treatment arm vs control on accuracy.
rationale: In the source study the AI Literacy Guide raised accuracy by 4.7 points (95% CI [0.2, 9.2]) and Automated Flagging by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3]), but the Guide result vanished without weights and the panel was online and U.S.-based. Effects may depend on age and digital familiarity, which the source did not stratify. This tests the Guide and automated flagging among respondents aged 55+, a group likely to have less experience with AI media.
contribution: Shows whether AI-discernment interventions generalise to older, less digitally experienced adults.
unresolved: Actual image and guide media files must be supplied by the research team
Full 12-post set and IRB number to be supplied

title: Feedback-based practice versus the AI Literacy Guide for spotting AI media
hypothesis: Practice with feedback raises accuracy more than the passive guide, which in turn does not differ from control.
primary_outcome: Share of 8 test posts correctly classified as AI-generated or authentic.
comparison: Practice-with-feedback vs guide vs control on test accuracy.
rationale: In the source study, passive pre-feed materials mostly did not help: the pooled accuracy effect was +1.0 point (95% CI [-0.3, +2.4]), and the AI Literacy Guide's +4.7 points had a CI that barely excluded zero. Automated flagging (+4.4) worked but needs external infrastructure. Active practice with immediate correctness feedback could teach detection without labels on each post.
contribution: Tests whether learning by practice with feedback beats passive literacy materials for AI-media discernment.
unresolved: The actual image and video files for the practice and test items must be supplied by the research team
